title: Building a Udemy Empire
overview: Jimmy Naraine, who has taught more than 500,000 students on Udemy and collected over 125,000 five-star ratings, set out to make online course creation feel simple and doable rather than glamorous. You got an honest picture of what Udemy is and is not good for, the mindset shifts that stop most experts from ever publishing, and his practical method: short minimum-viable courses, the Pajama Draft, listening to three- and four-star reviews, and stacking angles so your catalogue compounds. He closed by asking you to commit to one action in the next 72 hours.
key_ideas: Passive income from your expertise is real but not effortless. Jimmy still earns from courses he made 13 years ago, and while climbing a near-7,000-metre mountain in Argentina for two and a half weeks offline he sold around 1,500 courses. The catch: true passive income comes to people who do not over-optimise for it. People who only ask 'what can I publish to make money fastest' never last, because they are takers. Build an ecosystem of multiple courses, not one product, and combine it with the other things this summit teaches.

Most experts are held back by their nervous system, not by a lack of information. Jimmy shared his most embarrassing story: in 2017, already teaching tens of thousands, he dodged a call with Jay Shetty with excuses about bad Wi-Fi and travel because imposter syndrome told him he was not ready for a bigger arena. He calls this sophisticated hiding: living an impressive life full of seminars and travel while avoiding the uncomfortable things that matter, which are shipping, pitching and volunteering for the stage.

You do not need to be famous or young. Jimmy's father, a doctor who changed careers several times, said 'I'm in my 50s, what could I even teach?' He filmed his first course on an iPhone 4 with a basic lamp and a $20 microphone, it became a bestseller, and he now teaches over 200,000 people while keeping his full-time job. Course income is not binary between millionaire and bust; an extra $2,000 to $5,000 a month semi-passively is a perfectly good goal.

What Udemy actually is: a marketplace with 80 million students who already have their cards on file, free to register as an instructor, publishable within a day, and non-exclusive so you can sell elsewhere too. Coursera acquired Udemy this year and a combined marketplace could reach 290 million students. The downsides are real: you do not get students' email addresses directly, and it is a discount platform where buyers typically pay $15 to $25 (around $10 on Black Friday), so it is a volume game. Its biggest advantage is verified credibility: 125,000 public ratings on a big platform tells a stranger's nervous system 'this person is legit'. Relatability sells there; ordinary people buy from instructors they resonate with.

Treat Udemy as upgraded social media and build a Minimum Viable Product, not a monster. People pay for transformation, not for what you know: a thirsty person pays anything for water, and someone who wants to cross a river does not care about your two-year bridge, they will take the speedboat. Offered a 4-hour and a 24-hour course with equal ratings, almost everyone in the chat picked 4 hours. An MVP can be 40 to 60 minutes. His 14-Minute Confidence Guide started as a spontaneous 40-minute free course, grew with each round of reviews, and now has over 100,000 students and 7 to 8 hours of content. Five 45- to 60-minute courses in 12 months is a realistic target.

Listen to your three- and four-star reviews, not the five-star ones, because those people liked it but something was missing. When five or ten say the same thing, act; when students asked for PDF summaries he made them and ratings rose. Fall in love with testing: the year he filmed over a thousand videos nothing happened at first, then a little success, then compounding. You cannot predict which course will blow up, so publish several small ones, look at the data and put extra effort into the winner.

Ninety percent done but not published equals zero, or worse than zero, because you spent the time and gained nothing. Toxic perfectionism is his own weakness too, so he sets phone reminders to ship. Lower the pressure by remembering everything is a draft: you could publish a course tonight and unpublish it ten minutes later and nobody would know. Multiple angles also compound search: he has confidence courses for leaders, introverts, presenters and 'anxious and awkward' people, sharing 60 to 70 percent of the same core, so several show up on pages one and two. Go ultra-specific to trigger the buyer's reticular activating system; only established brands can afford generic titles.

Buyers judge the gate, not the hotel: they never see video 15 or 27, only your title, subtitle, biography, promo material and free preview videos, so both the entrance and the course itself must be excellent. Publishing builds an ecosystem: courses give you public proof to pitch conference organisers (send them free access so they see how you present in ten seconds), stages bring people who buy courses and ask for coaching and corporate training, and those clients buy more courses. His first one-to-one session was $150 and felt like too much; today engagements are 100 times that because visible credibility, trust and relatability change what people will pay. AI is scaffolding, not the building; nobody moves into scaffolding, they move into your personality, stories and experience. People want to learn from a human five years ahead of them, not a billionaire teaching budgeting. You will never feel 100 percent ready, so jump and trust the wings will develop.

frameworks.name: If I started today: Jimmy's course-building sequence
steps: Start with the avatar: if you struggle to find one, think of yourself 2, 3, 5 or 10 years ago and what you overcame
Define one clear transformation, taking them from where they are to where they want to be as fast as possible (the speedboat, not the bridge)
Reverse engineer: imagine you die tomorrow and have 60 to 90 minutes to teach that person only what they need, not everything you know
Write a basic curriculum and do not keep polishing it
Film the Pajama Draft from start to finish
Publish it as a Minimum Viable Product of 40 to 60 minutes
Read the three- and four-star reviews and add or revamp content when five or ten people say the same thing
Publish more courses with different angles on the same core so search compounds, then put extra effort into whichever one takes off

frameworks.name: The Pajama Draft
steps: Once you have a basic curriculum, put on pyjamas or something ridiculous so your nervous system knows this cannot be published
Set up your phone and a small microphone
Film the whole course from beginning to end; if you forget something, glance at your notes and keep going; if you make a mistake, breathe and keep going
Use it to see what works and what does not, shorten stories that run long, and prove to yourself you can speak your entire course out loud
Do it within the next 72 hours

frameworks.name: Building an ecosystem
steps: Publish multiple courses so you have students, reviews and data
Pitch conference organisers as a published teacher and send them free access to a course as living proof you can present
Speak on stages, where people discover you and buy your courses
Say yes when attendees ask for coaching, consulting or corporate training
Those clients then take your courses, so every part feeds the others and your rates rise with your visible credibility

quotes.text: People will not pay you for what you know. People will pay you for the transformation, whatever it is that they want.

quotes.speaker: Jimmy Naraine
quotes.text: No one will move into a scaffolding. People move into a real building.

quotes.speaker: Jimmy Naraine
quotes.text: If you wait until you feel 100% ready, you will never do anything massive.

exercises: Write down what has been holding you back from publishing a course: fear, self-doubt, overwhelm or not knowing where to start.
Thought experiment: two courses on the same topic with equally great ratings, one 4 hours and one 24 hours. Notice which you would pick, and design your own course accordingly.
Find your avatar by thinking about yourself 2, 3, 5 or 10 years ago: what did you struggle with that you have since overcome? Teach the previous version of you.
Imagine you will die tomorrow and have only 60 to 90 minutes to teach that person everything they need to reach their goal. Build your curriculum from that.
Film a Pajama Draft of your whole course in the next 72 hours, and commit to it publicly in the chat or by messaging Jimmy on social media.
Screenshot the six summary slides shown at the end of the session.
Commit to one concrete action from this talk, or any talk at the summit, within 72 hours, and tell Jimmy or someone in the community so they can hold you accountable.
next_steps: Choose one specific avatar (your past self) and one transformation, and write a 60- to 90-minute curriculum for it, nothing more.
Film your Pajama Draft start to finish within 72 hours, phone and $20 microphone only.

Register a free Udemy instructor account and publish a 40- to 60-minute MVP, with a specific title, subtitle, bio and a couple of free preview videos, remembering it is only a draft you can change or unpublish.
Anything sitting 90 percent finished on your hard drive: ship it this week, then read the three- and four-star feedback to decide what to improve.
attribution_notes: Lines labelled with Jimmy Naraine's name were attributed to him (the transcript spelt it 'Naren' in the introduction); lines labelled 'Mindvalley' were the host Jason Goldberg's introduction and closing remarks, including his own story about turning a one-person live event into a one-to-one session.
